Open-book reference: Machines Ch1–9 (full course)

Covers every chapter, Ch1 to Ch9, and replaces the short Ch1–3 strip of the earlier version. All phasors are rms and per phase unless marked “3ph”. Subscript 1 = phase (, ), subscript L = line (, ). Machines and transformers are star-connected unless the question says otherwise, and ratings are line V, line I and total (3ph) power. p = pole-PAIRS (course notation): . = angle of the current relative to the voltage, so lag means . Exam: 120 min, open book, 4 × 20 marks. Q1 = Ch1–2, Q2 = Ch3, Q3 = Ch7 with Ch4–5 basics in (a), Q4 = Ch8 and per-unit, with Q4c words only. Every check value below was recomputed in Python.

Constants: H/m · m/s² · (Ωm)⁻¹ · · · 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ · cm² = m² · mm² = m².

Ch1 Review of power and energy

Energy conversion (1.2). Transformer: AC electrical in, AC electrical out (changes V and I). Machine: electrical ↔︎ mechanical through magnetic fields. Motor: electrical in, mechanical out. Generator: the reverse. Machines are reversible. Gears and pulleys are “mechanical transformers”.

Why efficiency matters (1.7.4): (1) limited stored energy (EV range), (2) running cost (lifetime electricity cost is many times the purchase price), (3) cooling (the loss becomes heat, and temperature rise limits rating). IEC 60034-30-1 sets minimum efficiency classes; larger motors are more efficient.

Power-factor correction (2.5). A capacitor in parallel with the load generates Q locally. P, and the load’s own V, I, P, Q, are unchanged. The supply Q, S and current fall, and the supply pf rises towards 1. Over-correction past unity makes the pf leading and the current rise again, so one target pf has two C values (under- and over-corrected).

Unity pf: . Reverse problem (C given): , , pf , lead/lag from the sign of . Why it is useful: lower current, lower cable and transformer loading and loss, lower VA charges.

Equivalent-circuit parameter tests (2.6). Measure V, I, P; then , (inductive), then the series or parallel formulas above. The two models give different numbers for the same data: 240 V, 4 A, 500 W gives series but parallel . 3ph: per phase first (, ). The transformer OC/SC tests (Ch3) and IM tests (Ch7) are this method.

Saturation and leakage (3.5): above about 1.6–2 T (knee 1.2–1.7 T for silicon steel) collapses towards 1. Extra mmf buys almost no extra flux. With AC, V fixes the flux (sinusoidal), so the current becomes large and peaky and the winding overheats. This sets the voltage rating, and and constant L both fail. Leakage flux links one winding only, which gives , . Hysteresis loop: remanence , coercivity ; loop area = hysteresis energy per m³ per cycle.

Three-phase transformers (3.8.9): treat as three single-phase units in star. Per phase: , , solve the single-phase circuit, then ×3 all powers and losses and ×√3 for line voltages. “5 % above rated output voltage”: (16 kV: 9.699 kV).

Special transformers (3.11): isolation (1:1, unearthed supply, medical); voltage (potential) transformer, e.g. 11 kV:110 V; current transformer, e.g. 10 kA:5 A with a 1-turn primary needs 2000 secondary turns; autotransformer (Variac): one winding with a moving wiper, no isolation, 0 to about 280 V. RCD (safety switch): trips when active and neutral currents differ by tens of mA; it does not protect against active-to-neutral contact or a fault with no earth path. High-frequency model and electronic transformers: not examinable.

Ch6 Rotating fields

  • Each phase is a pair of opposite coils. The three magnetic axes are 120° apart. Positive current gives a field along the axis and negative current reverses it. This gives 6 field directions, which step round to make a stepwise rotating field (stepper motor, not examinable).
  • Balanced 3ph currents give a field of constant magnitude rotating at constant speed .
  • Phase sequence sets the direction: abc = bca = cab one way, acb = cba = bac the other. Swapping any two supply leads reverses rotation. A cyclic relabelling of all three does not.
  • One electrical cycle moves the field one pole-pair, which is of a revolution. Hence .
  • A single-phase winding gives a pulsating field (forward plus backward rotating), so the starting torque is zero. It needs an auxiliary winding and capacitor to start (not examinable).

Sign conventions (lead/lag, over/under-excited):

Case Current Excitation Q Phasor
Generator, lagging output behind over-excited delivers Q long, δ small
Generator, leading output ahead of under-excited absorbs Q short, δ large, low

Motor, lagging input behind under-excited absorbs Q

Rule: over-excited generates Q, under-excited absorbs Q, in either mode. is generating, is motoring. The mechanical input (steam valve) sets P and δ. The field current sets , and so Q.

V-curve (constant P): against is a V, with its minimum at pf = 1. A larger P moves the V up and to the right. Say “generates Q / absorbs Q” rather than lead or lag. Slide 8.6.4 labels pf from the supply side.

Construction facts: round rotor for 2 or 4 poles (thermal plants); salient pole for 4 poles and up (hydro, low speed). PM rotors are mostly used in motors, wound-field rotors in generators. Efficiency is up to 98 %. To synchronise, match the phase sequence, frequency, voltage magnitude and phase. Close the contactor when the lamps are dark. Not self-starting on a fixed-frequency supply (average torque zero at standstill).

Ch9 Power systems introduction

Part Rating Notes
1. Generation 3ph synchronous generators, 10–25 kV coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, wind, solar; often near the energy source
2. Transmission 3ph, 115–800 kV (SA: 275 kV, 132 kV) high V for efficiency: , loss
3. Distribution 3ph, 2.4–69 kV (SA: 66, 33, 11 kV) within the city
4. Loads domestic 1ph 240 V (safety); commercial/industrial 3ph 415 V to several kV industrial loads mostly induction motors
5. Market National Electricity Market (AEMO)

Transmission system (9.1.3): drawn as a single-line diagram (one line represents 3ph). A busbar is a node where every point is at the same (nominal) voltage. Generators and lines are paralleled for reliability (one can fail), maintenance without interrupting supply, and running the most efficient number of generators for the demand.

Scale numbers: household about 2 kW; SA demand typically about 3000 MW; largest coal, nuclear, hydro stations about 1000 MW; large wind turbine 2–5 MW each. Torrens Island: 1963, gas, 8 turbines, 1280 MW. Pelican Point: 2000, gas, 2 turbines, 485 MW, 53 % efficient. Demand peaks in the evening; off-peak water heating fills the night.

Generation (9.2): via mechanical power: thermal (coal, gas, nuclear, geothermal, biomass, solar thermal → steam → turbine), water (hydro, tidal, wave) or wind. Direct: solar cells (silicon, tens of kW up to tens of MW) and fuel cells (hydrogen + oxygen → electricity; electrolysis is the reverse). Conventional plants: reliable, cheap to run, controllable, but limited fuel (gas tens of years, coal hundreds) and waste (CO₂ and global warming; sulphur and nitrogen oxides and acid rain; nuclear waste). Renewables: “unlimited” resource and zero emissions in operation, but difficulties are economic (cost, government support), technical (variability of wind, surviving storms) and environmental (visual impact, noise).

PQ9.1 answers: (a) advantages of electric power: made from many sources, transmitted long distances, easily converted to other forms, many applications. (b) sources: oil, gas, coal, nuclear, hydro, tidal, wave, wind, solar, geothermal. (c) fossil-fuel issues: finite resources, greenhouse gas emissions and pollution. (d) high voltage: for a fixed power the current is inversely proportional to voltage and the loss goes with current squared, so loss falls (doubling V quarters the loss). (e) lines are paralleled for reliability and maintenance.

Traps

Ch1

  • rpm in . Convert with first.
  • Treating the motor rating as input power. It is the shaft output: .
  • Using with phase quantities or 3 with line quantities.
  • Quoting pf without “lead” or “lag”.
  • Peak vs rms: the 4.44 equation and every power formula use rms V and I (peak B).

Ch2

  • Forgetting the conjugate in (flips the sign of Q).
  • Adding magnitudes ( V) instead of phasors ().
  • Adding apparent powers of loads. Add P’s and Q’s.
  • Taking the sign of Q from the square root. L or lag is +, C or lead is −.
  • Using (parallel) when the question wants series R, or the reverse.
  • Battery load power as or loss as . They are and .
  • Putting across a star phase. The supply figure is always line.
  • PFC: using for star capacitors, using 50 Hz when the supply is 60 Hz, giving as positive, or thinking P changes.
  • Atan quadrant: if Re < 0, add 180°.

Ch3

  • cm² → m² is ; mm → m is ; radius vs diameter.
  • Missing the second gap or the second pole face (2 × 0.07 mm, 10 cm²).
  • Putting reluctance or in the back-emf equation.
  • Rounding N down (B then exceeds the limit).
  • Scaling the total iron loss with one law. Split into hysteresis and eddy first.
  • instead of ; referring in the wrong direction.
  • Series formulas on the OC test (gives a series R, X, not ).
  • Forgetting per phase on 3ph tests (, ).
  • with or with ; forgetting the ×3 for 3ph losses.
  • Using ’s line value in the per-phase KVL, or forgetting when the line voltage is asked.
  • Lead sign: a load generating Q has a leading current, .
  • Saying is in phase with for a resistive load. It lags.

Ch4

  • Taking p as poles in . 6-pole at 50 Hz is 1000 rpm, not 500.
  • Rounding to the nearest integer instead of down, for an induction machine.
  • Taking part-load power as . It is .
  • Scaling the rated speed in proportion. The speed drop (DC) or slip speed (IM) stays constant.
  • Changing f without V on an AC machine (saturation). “Safe” means V and f together.

Ch5

  • Using rpm in .
  • Taking . It is .
  • Using for generator efficiency. It is , with .

Ch6

  • Thinking a cyclic relabelling reverses rotation. Only swapping two leads does.
  • Saying a single-phase field rotates. It pulsates.

Ch7

  • Putting the line voltage into the per-phase circuit. That makes every power ×3.
  • Dividing by ω. Use ; only goes with ω.
  • Taking rotor Cu as . That is ; rotor Cu is .
  • Adding as magnitudes.
  • Taking the slip at the rated speed when another operating speed is given.
  • Rounding s early (0.02 vs 0.02222 is 11 % in ).
  • Using line values in the tests. Apply and first. , not .
  • Using in . Thinking extra rotor R raises (it moves it).
  • Dropping the minus signs in generator mode. Angles near ±180° are correct.
  • V/f: scaling only V. Also scale X and .

Ch8

  • Using the OC line voltage as a phase voltage. That makes √3 too big.
  • Answering in Ω when pu is asked, or the reverse (Jun23 asks Ω, Jun24 asks pu).
  • Computing with phase V and total VA.
  • Treating MW as MVA. .
  • Using V = 1 when the question says ±x % of rated.
  • Wrong sign on the current angle. Lead is pf; a wrong sign gives 2.41 pu instead of 1.634 in Jun24 4b.
  • Using with a motor’s input current.
  • Recomputing for . Also forgetting to state δ = 90°.
  • Using instead of in the capability triangle.
  • Leaving “lag” or “lead” off the final pf.

Ch9

  • Saying high voltage “increases power”. It reduces current, so loss (and conductor size) for the same power.
  • Mixing up the voltage levels: generation 10–25 kV, transmission 115–800 kV, distribution 2.4–69 kV, domestic 240 V.
  • Listing only one renewable difficulty. Give economic, technical and environmental.

Short-answer points

Words only. About one mark per point; give 3–5 per part.

Ch1–2 (Q1, and Q4c has asked these)

  • Real, reactive, apparent power (Jun24 4c(i)): P comes from the current in phase with V; it is the average of instantaneous power, net energy to the load, does useful work, absorbed by resistors. Q comes from the quadrature current; energy oscillates between source and load with zero mean; inductors absorb it, capacitors generate it; no useful work but needs current. S is the magnitude of complex power (real part P, imaginary part Q), equals V × total I, and sets ratings. P and Q are both scalars.
  • PFC (Jun23 4c(i)): loads (mainly induction motors) draw Q, which is energy oscillating in the system. It loads generators, transformers and lines and adds losses. A parallel capacitor (or over-excited sync motor) generates Q locally, so the supply Q, S and current fall. P and the load are unchanged. Tariffs on VA make it pay.
  • Why three-phase: a balanced 3ph winding makes a constant rotating field, so machines self-start; total instantaneous power is constant (smooth, quiet); better use of material and conductors.
  • Why efficiency matters: limited stored energy (EVs), running cost over the life, and heat removal limits the rating.

Ch3 (Q2, quiz and test last questions)

  • Choosing primary turns (2023 quiz Q7): the back-emf equation links turns and peak flux for a given V and f; choose turns so B is just below saturation. Too few: B too high, saturation, high and distorted current, overheating. Too many: low B, more winding R, more copper loss, lower η, possible overheating.
  • Ideal vs real, load R doubled (2024 test Q8): ideal: V set only by input V and turns ratio, so unchanged; current halves (Ohm’s law). Real: series R and leakage X drop less voltage at lower current, so V rises slightly; current falls to slightly more than half.
  • Transformer losses (Jun24 4c(ii)): copper loss: heating of the windings, series winding R, varies with the square of output. Iron loss: hysteresis (domain reversal) and eddy currents (induced core currents), core-loss resistance in the shunt branch, constant with load (set by V and f). Max η where they are equal.
  • phase, resistive load (Jun23 2c(iii)): lags, because the series reactance makes the current lag and the load voltage is in phase with the current.
  • OC voltage halved (Jun24 2c(iii)): fixed shunt impedance: current ×0.5, P and Q ×0.25, pf ×1. A real core draws even less current (further below the knee).
  • Transformer no-load current not zero: magnetising current (finite permeability, , lags 90°) plus core-loss current (hysteresis and eddy, , in phase). Saturation makes it large and distorted at high V.
  • Airgap effect: μr = 1, so even a short gap dominates the reluctance; L falls, more current for the same flux, but L becomes linear; most energy and the force are in the gap; in an IM the gap is unavoidable, so it is kept small (magnetising current, pf).
  • Laminations and silicon steel: thin insulated laminations break eddy-current paths; silicon raises resistivity and lowers hysteresis loss.

Ch7 (Q4c has asked these)

  • IM no-load current not zero (Jun24 4c(iii)): magnetising current sets up the airgap flux, and is large because of the airgap (). A core-loss component covers hysteresis and eddy currents (). Friction (bearings) and windage (air, fan) need a little power, so there is a small slip and rotor current. The pf is low.
  • Perfectly conducting rotor, (Jun23 4c(iii)): no rotor loss, so higher efficiency. , so the curve is vertical at , like a synchronous machine. Zero starting torque.
  • Transformer vs IM (Jun23 4c(ii)): both have primary and secondary windings on a magnetic core, both run on 3ph AC, with similar circuits. The IM secondary rotates and is short-circuited, the rotor frequency is , the rotor R is divided by s, and the airgap makes the magnetising current much larger.
  • Torque production: rotating field at ; slip induces slip-frequency emf in the shorted rotor; rotor currents in the field give force; at no change of flux, so no emf, current or torque.
  • V/f control: frequency sets ; flux ; reducing f alone saturates the core (large current); keeping V/f constant keeps flux and , so the curve slides along the speed axis; small boost at low f for the drop.
  • Tests: DC test gives ; no-load (s ≈ 0) gives , (includes friction and windage); blocked rotor (s = 1, low V) gives and X; split X equally.
  • Wound rotor and external R: raises and starting torque, lowers starting current, unchanged; extra rotor loss, so cut it out at speed.
  • IM as generator: driven above , s < 0, negative, power reverses; still absorbs Q for magnetising; cannot control its own Q or voltage; suits wind and regenerative braking.

Ch8

  • Sync machine advantages: exact speed, high efficiency, and controllable Q (unlike an IM).
  • Induction vs synchronous: sync runs exactly at , IM below it with slip rising with load; sync rotor field from DC or magnets, IM rotor currents induced; IM always absorbs Q (lagging), sync Q set by field current; IM self-starting, cheap, robust.
  • Industrial pf lagging, why sync motors: plants are mostly induction motors, which absorb Q; VA tariffs and cable loading; an over-excited sync motor generates Q while driving its load; limited to .
  • Field current on an infinite bus: V and f fixed by the system; P set by the turbine; sets and Q; over-excited delivers Q (lagging), under-excited absorbs Q (leading, larger δ, less stable); V-curve minimum at unity pf.
  • Q capability limit: stator current heating (, so ), rotor field heating on the over-excited side, stability (δ → 90°) on the under-excited side.
  • Per-unit advantages: values relative to rating show size at a glance; similar machines have similar pu values (easy error check); no √3 or 3, line = phase; transformer impedances the same on both sides.
  • Salient vs round rotor: low speed (hydro) needs many poles, easy with salient poles, low stress; high speed (2–4 poles, 3000 rpm) needs a strong round rotor with slotted winding, low windage.
  • Not self-starting: at standstill the field sweeps past and the torque alternates each half cycle, average zero; start with a pony motor, damper (starting) cage or an inverter ramp.
  • Sync vs DC circuit: both an emf proportional to speed and field behind a series impedance; DC uses R and DC quantities; sync uses mainly and phasors, where δ controls P and controls Q.

Ch9

  • High-voltage transmission: same power, current ; loss , so loss falls with ; thinner conductors, less voltage drop; transformers make stepping cheap.
  • Paralleled lines and generators: reliability (fault tolerance), maintenance without interrupting supply, run the most efficient number of generators.
  • Renewables: unlimited resource, zero operating emissions; but economic (cost, subsidies), technical (variability, storms) and environmental (visual, noise) difficulties.
  • Fossil fuels: finite reserves; CO₂ (global warming), SOₓ and NOₓ (acid rain); nuclear has radioactive waste.
